title: JavaScript array methods versus C# LINQ
hook: LINQ and JavaScript array methods solve the same problems — filter, map, aggregate — but LINQ on IEnumerable is lazy and composes deferred queries; JavaScript array methods run eagerly and allocate new arrays each step.

blocks.text: **C# LINQ** provides **query syntax** (`from x in xs where ... select`) and **method syntax** (`.Where().Select()`). Operates on **IEnumerable<T>** with **deferred execution** until enumeration. **JavaScript** array methods operate on **Array** in memory — **eager**, return new arrays (except reduce to scalar). **IQueryable** adds expression trees for remote providers (SQL) — no direct JS equivalent except query builders (Prisma, ORM). **Async LINQ** (IAsyncEnumerable) maps to **async generators** in JS.

entries.plainDefinition: LINQ builds query plan; runs on foreach/ToList — not on Where call.
entries.example: var q = list.Where(x => x > 0); // not executed yet

entries.plainDefinition: Force full evaluation — ToList, ToArray, Sum terminal in LINQ; array methods always materialize.
entries.example: JS filter already returns new array — materialized.

entries.plainDefinition: LINQ provider translates expression to SQL — remote execution.
function* yields lazy sequence — closer to IEnumerable lazy pull.
entries.example: function* range(n) { for (let i=0;i<n;i++) yield i; }

blocks.text: Full-stack engineers translate mental models between tiers — **Select** is **map**, **Where** is **filter**, **Aggregate** is **reduce**, **SelectMany** is **flatMap**, **GroupBy** is **Object.groupBy**. Misunderstanding laziness causes double enumeration bugs in C# and unnecessary triple allocation in JS chains. Senior interviews ask when to fuse JS loops vs keep LINQ deferred.

blocks.title: Interview trap: multiple enumeration
blocks.body: LINQ deferred query re-runs predicate on each foreach if not materialized. JS array already materialized — each method pass is explicit O(n).

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Lazy in JS
items.body: Use generator + for-of or iterator helpers — not native on Array.

diagram.title: Eager JS vs lazy LINQ
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  subgraph JS[Eager JS chain]
    A1[array] --> F1[filter new array]
    F1 --> M1[map new array]
    M1 --> R1[reduce value]
  end
  subgraph LINQ[Lazy LINQ]
    Q[query object] --> E[enumerate once]
    E --> T[terminal Sum/ToList]
  end

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming JS filter/map is lazy like LINQ. Double enumerating expensive LINQ without ToList. Using LINQ to Objects expecting SQL translation. Chaining many eager JS passes on megabyte arrays without fusion.

blocks.text: Choose **IQueryable** when provider translates to SQL; **IEnumerable** in-memory like JS arrays. JS **Iterator helpers** (ES2024 Stage) add lazy filter/map on iterables. For Node bulk data, **streams** are push-based LINQ-like pipelines. Benchmark: one fused for-loop vs chain on 1M rows — know numbers order-of-magnitude, not memorize.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying map/filter are lazy. Cannot map LINQ operators to JS methods. Unaware double enumeration cost in deferred LINQ.

interviewTakeaways: JS array methods eager; LINQ IEnumerable lazy until terminal.
Materialize LINQ once with ToList if reusing query; JS each step allocates.
60s: Same functional vocabulary different execution. JS chains scan multiple times. LINQ defers. Generators/iterators for lazy JS. IQueryable for SQL — no JS twin.
Follow-up: when would you fuse three JS array passes into one loop?
commonPitfalls: Treating JavaScript map/filter as lazy deferred queries.
Double enumeration of expensive LINQ without caching.
Strong answer: operator mapping table, eager vs lazy, generators, IQueryable distinction.

jsTsCorrelations.note: TS types for generators enable lazy pipelines typed similarly to IEnumerable<T> consumption.
async function* parallels IAsyncEnumerable — await for each in loop like foreach await in C#.
